Triggers.value: Specific body parts associated with the event
People who are related to the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: make sure to stay close to exit
I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself
Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

issues.item: Triggers: Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
issues.explanation: The loss-themed trigger is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner. It implies bereavement-related activation, but there are no corresponding memory, threat, or appraisal items about death, losing a loved one, or grief. In this profile it stands out as clinically mismatched rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: Avoiding authority figures or uniforms is not well linked to the reported trauma type or the rest of the profile. For intimate-partner physical abuse, this strategy would need supporting material suggesting the perpetrator was an authority figure or that uniforms became trauma cues, but no such trigger, threat, memory, or appraisal items are present. It therefore looks disconnected from the formulation and symptom pattern.

vignette:
Rangi is a 63-year-old Māori man, widowed, who has worked in construction for the better part of four decades. He came to his first intake appointment with the quiet, careful bearing of someone who has spent a long time trying to take up as little space as possible - a quality that sits strangely against his large frame and weathered hands. His PCL-5 score of 68 places him in the severe range, and the picture that emerged across the first few sessions was one of a man whose interior life had been quietly dismantled over years of abuse by his late wife, and who had only recently begun to understand that what happened to him had a name.

The abuse began gradually, as it so often does, and escalated over more than a decade. His wife's attacks were physical - striking, grabbing, once fracturing two of his fingers when she slammed a door on his hand during an argument. What Rangi remembers most vividly is the specific geography of those moments: her hands around his wrist, the particular angle of an arm raised, the sight of bruising on his own forearms in the bathroom mirror the following morning. He never called the police. He told no one. He was, he believed, supposed to be able to handle it.

She died of a cardiac event three years ago, and it was in the silence that followed that the symptoms arrived in full. Now, at work on a construction site, Rangi finds that certain visual details carry an almost physical charge. What he carries onto the site each morning is not merely memory but a persistent, bodily sense that danger has not passed - that the world remains the kind of place where harm comes from the people closest to you. Living at that pitch of alertness, he finds the site dense with signals his nervous system cannot stop reading: a raised forearm, a sharp gesture, his own bruised knuckles after a hard day's work all arrive already charged, because his body has decided, before any of it happens, that threat is present. A co-worker's forearm raised to wipe sweat from a brow, a supervisor gesturing sharply during a briefing, even the sight of his own hands at the end of a shift - these images land with a force disproportionate to their content, pulling him back into the sensory texture of the abuse. When the crew talks at lunch and someone mentions a domestic dispute they heard about on the news, Rangi goes quiet and finds a reason to leave the table. People who knew him and his wife - a brother-in-law who still calls occasionally, a neighbour from the old street - have become almost impossible to be around; their presence makes the past feel present in a way he cannot manage.

When these triggers catch him off-guard, Rangi's first instinct is to move. But it is not only the triggers themselves that drive this - it is the unrelenting sense of threat that underlies every hour of his day. When the world feels that dangerous, positioning himself near exits and scanning every room he enters is not a symptom he can name; it is simply what a person does to stay safe. The spending, the conflict avoidance, the careful management of who he is around - all of it flows from the same source: a felt conviction that he cannot afford to be caught off-guard again. He has made a habit of positioning himself near doors - on the site, in the canteen, in any room he enters - scanning for exits the moment he walks in, a behaviour so automatic now he barely notices it until a colleague comments on it. He also spends money in ways he cannot always account for: tools he doesn't need, takeaway meals, a new television he barely watches. He understands, dimly, that he is trying to fill something or outrun something, but the spending brings a few hours of relief before the flatness returns. And he avoids conflict with a rigidity that has begun to cost him professionally - he has declined to raise legitimate safety concerns on site, has let errors go unchallenged, has been passed over for a foreman role he was qualified for because, as his site manager noted, he "doesn't push back."

The avoidance has fed something darker. Because Rangi never talks about what happened, never allows himself to be around those connected to it, the events remain unprocessed and close to the surface - and the triggers, when they come, feel as raw as ever. He wakes in the night, alert and listening, certain for a moment that he is not safe, and lies still until he has checked the room. He startles at sounds on the site - a dropped beam, a shout across the yard - in ways that embarrass him deeply. And that embarrassment compounds what has become his most corrosive belief: that he is weak. A real man, he tells himself, would not have let this happen, and would not still be undone by it. He cannot rely on himself to stay steady, to react normally, to be the person he was before. He feels, much of the time, dead inside - not grief exactly, but an absence where feeling used to be.

What finally brought Rangi to seek help was his youngest daughter, who visited recently and told him, plainly, that she was frightened for him. He sat with that for two weeks before making the call. What he is most afraid of, he said at the end of the first session, is that the man he used to be is simply gone. What he hopes, more quietly, is that someone might tell him he is wrong.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that Rangi's sense of threat directly drives or leads to his maladaptive strategies (e.g., exit-scanning, avoidance, spending); the strategies are linked to triggers catching him off-guard, not to an ongoing perceived threat.

No paragraph conveys that Rangi's sense of threat causes or activates his triggers; the vignette describes triggers arising from environmental cues at work and social situations, but does not establish that a felt sense of threat produces or amplifies those triggering stimuli.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Threat → Maladaptive Strategies: No paragraph conveys that Rangi's sense of threat directly drives or leads to his maladaptive strategies (e.g., exit-scanning, avoidance, spending); the strategies are linked to triggers catching him off-guard, not to an ongoing perceived threat.
  e.g. "When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible."
  e.g. "She had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed her body to settle enough to sleep, so she checked them twice."
  e.g. "The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong."
- Threat → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that Rangi's sense of threat causes or activates his triggers; the vignette describes triggers arising from environmental cues at work and social situations, but does not establish that a felt sense of threat produces or amplifies those triggering stimuli.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
